Lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair repulsion, hence CH$_4$ (109.5°) > NH$_3$ (107°) > H$_2$O (104.5°).

Molecular orbital theory

  • Order (up to N$_2$): $\sigma1s < \sigma^*1s < \sigma2s < \sigma^*2s < \pi2p_x = \pi2p_y < \sigma2p_z < \pi^*2p_x = \pi^*2p_y < \sigma^*2p_z$. For O$_2$, F$_2$: $\sigma2p_z$ comes before $\pi2p$.
  • Bond order $= \dfrac{N_b - N_a}{2}$. Higher bond order → shorter bond, higher bond enthalpy.
  • Bond orders: N$_2$ 3, O$_2$ 2, O$_2^+$ 2.5, O$_2^-$ 1.5, O$_2^{2-}$ 1, He$_2$ 0 (does not exist), CO 3, NO 2.5.
  • Paramagnetic (unpaired electrons): O$_2$, O$_2^+$, O$_2^-$, B$_2$, NO. Diamagnetic: N$_2$, F$_2$, CO, C$_2$.

Polarity & dipole moment

  • Zero dipole (symmetric): CO$_2$, BF$_3$, CCl$_4$, CH$_4$, SF$_6$, XeF$_4$, PCl$_5$, trans isomers.
  • Non-zero: H$_2$O, NH$_3$, SO$_2$, CHCl$_3$, NF$_3$ (small), cis isomers. NH$_3$ > NF$_3$ because lone pair moment adds in NH$_3$.
  • Fajans' rules: small cation, large anion, high charge → more covalent character.

Hydrogen bonding

Only with F, O, N. HF has the strongest H-bond; H$_2$O has more H-bonds per molecule (higher b.p. than HF). Intramolecular H-bonding: o-nitrophenol, salicylaldehyde (lower b.p., more volatile).

Sigma & pi bonds

Single bond = 1σ; double = 1σ + 1π; triple = 1σ + 2π. Count carefully in organic molecules.

Exam tip

2–3 questions: shape/hybridisation of a molecule, bond order or magnetic nature from MOT, dipole moment comparison. The tables above cover almost everything asked.

questions.q: The shape of SF$_6$ molecule is
questions.explanation: S has 6 bond pairs, no lone pairs: sp$^3$d$^2$, octahedral, bond angle 90°.
questions.trick: 6 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → sp$^3$d$^2$, octahedral — straight from VSEPR count.

questions.q: The bond order of O$_2^-$ (superoxide ion) is
questions.explanation: O$_2$ has bond order 2 (10 bonding, 6 antibonding). Adding one electron to $\pi^*$ gives $(10-7)/2 = 1.5$.
questions.trick: For BO use $(N_b-N_a)/2$; O$_2^-$ adds one antibonding electron to O$_2$'s BO 2.

questions.q: Which of the following molecules is paramagnetic?
questions.explanation: O$_2$ has two unpaired electrons in the degenerate $\pi^*2p$ orbitals. This was a triumph of MO theory.
questions.trick: Unpaired electrons in $\pi^*2p$ → paramagnetic; only O$_2$ here qualifies.

questions.q: The hybridisation of carbon atoms in ethene (C$_2$H$_4$) is
questions.explanation: Each C forms three σ bonds (two C–H, one C–C) and one π bond: sp$^2$, planar, 120°.
questions.trick: 3 $\sigma$ bonds + 1 $\pi$ around each C → sp$^2$, planar 120°.

questions.q: The number of lone pairs on the central atom and the shape of XeF$_4$ are
questions.explanation: Xe: 8 valence electrons, 4 used in bonds, 2 lone pairs remain. sp$^3$d$^2$ with lone pairs axial (opposite) → square planar.
questions.trick: Xe: 8 valence e$^-$, 4 in bonds → 2 lone pairs, axial → square planar.

questions.q: Which of the following has zero dipole moment?
questions.explanation: CO$_2$ is linear (O=C=O); the two bond dipoles cancel. H$_2$O is bent, NH$_3$ pyramidal, HCl a polar diatomic.
questions.trick: Symmetric linear O=C=O → bond dipoles cancel → zero net dipole.

questions.q: The correct order of bond angles is
questions.explanation: More lone pairs → more repulsion → smaller bond angle: 109.5° > 107° > 104.5°.
questions.trick: More lone pairs → more repulsion → smaller angle: 109.5°>107°>104.5°.

questions.q: Among the hydrogen halides, the highest boiling point is shown by
questions.explanation: HF molecules are strongly hydrogen-bonded. Order: HF > HI > HBr > HCl (the last three by van der Waals forces).
questions.trick: H-bonding dominates: HF is the outlier with by far the highest b.p.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT isoelectronic with N$_2$?
questions.explanation: N$_2$, CO, CN$^-$ and NO$^+$ all have 14 electrons and bond order 3. O$_2$ has 16 electrons.
questions.trick: Isoelectronic with N$_2$ means 14 electrons; O$_2$ has 16, so it's the odd one out.

questions.q: The number of σ and π bonds in acetylene (HC≡CH) are respectively
questions.explanation: Two C–H σ bonds + one C–C σ bond = 3 σ; the triple bond contributes 2 π.
questions.trick: Count $\sigma$ bonds by skeleton (each bond has exactly one), extra bonds are all $\pi$.

questions.q: The shape of ClF$_3$ is
questions.explanation: Cl has 3 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs (sp$^3$d). Lone pairs occupy equatorial positions → T-shape.
questions.trick: 3 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs (sp$^3$d), lone pairs equatorial → T-shape.

questions.q: Which has the highest lattice enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Lattice enthalpy ∝ (charge product)/(distance). MgO has 2+/2− ions and the smallest size among the doubly charged options.
questions.trick: Lattice enthalpy $\propto$ (charge product)/(distance); smallest 2+/2− pair wins.

questions.q: The species with bond order 2.5 is
questions.explanation: Removing an antibonding electron from O$_2$ (BO 2) increases bond order to 2.5. O$_2^+$ has a shorter, stronger bond than O$_2$.
questions.trick: Removing an antibonding electron raises bond order; O$_2^+$ = 2 + 0.5 = 2.5.

questions.q: In ozone (O$_3$), the two O–O bond lengths are equal because of
questions.explanation: O$_3$ is a resonance hybrid of two structures; each bond has partial double-bond character (bond length 128 pm, between 121 and 148 pm).
questions.trick: Equal, intermediate bond lengths signal resonance, not a fixed single/double bond.

questions.q: Which of the following molecules has the largest dipole moment?
questions.explanation: BF$_3$ and CH$_4$ are symmetric (zero). In NH$_3$ the lone-pair moment and N–H moments point the same way; in NF$_3$ they oppose, so NH$_3$ (1.47 D) > NF$_3$ (0.23 D).
questions.trick: Lone-pair moment adds to bond moments in NH$_3$ but opposes them in NF$_3$.

questions.q: According to Fajans' rules, covalent character is favoured by
questions.explanation: A small, highly charged cation strongly polarises a large, easily polarised anion → covalent character (e.g. LiI more covalent than LiF).
questions.trick: Fajans: small, highly charged cation + large anion → more covalent character.

questions.q: The shape of PCl$_5$ molecule is
questions.explanation: P has 5 bond pairs and no lone pairs: sp$^3$d hybridisation gives a trigonal bipyramidal shape.
questions.trick: 5 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → sp$^3$d, trigonal bipyramidal.

questions.q: The shape of SF$_4$ molecule is
questions.explanation: S has 4 bond pairs + 1 lone pair (sp$^3$d, AB$_4$E type). The lone pair occupies an equatorial position, giving a see-saw shape.
questions.trick: AB$_4$E (sp$^3$d), lone pair equatorial → see-saw shape.

questions.q: The shape of the triiodide ion I$_3^-$ is
questions.explanation: Central I has 2 bond pairs + 3 lone pairs (AB$_2$E$_3$, sp$^3$d). The three lone pairs occupy equatorial positions, forcing a linear shape.
questions.trick: AB$_2$E$_3$ (sp$^3$d): 3 lone pairs equatorial forces the shape linear.

questions.q: The shape of BrF$_5$ molecule is
questions.explanation: Br has 5 bond pairs + 1 lone pair (AB$_5$E, sp$^3$d$^2$). The lone pair pushes the 5 F atoms into a square pyramidal arrangement.
questions.trick: AB$_5$E (sp$^3$d$^2$): one lone pair pushes 5 bonds into square pyramidal.

questions.q: The hybridisation of Xe in XeF$_2$ is
questions.explanation: Xe has 2 bond pairs + 3 lone pairs, requiring 5 electron domains, i.e. sp$^3$d hybridisation (linear AB$_2$E$_3$ shape).
questions.trick: 2 bond pairs + 3 lone pairs = 5 domains → sp$^3$d, linear shape.

questions.q: In the most stable Lewis structure of the nitrate ion NO$_3^-$ (one N=O and two N–O bonds), the formal charge on the nitrogen atom is
questions.explanation: Formal charge $= 5 - 0 - 8/2 = +1$ for N, which forms 4 bonds (1 double + 2 single) around it in this resonance structure, consistent with the overall $-1$ charge on the ion.
questions.trick: Formal charge $= V - L - B/2$; compute per atom in the drawn Lewis structure.

questions.q: In BF$_3$, boron has how many electrons around it, making it an exception to the octet rule?
questions.explanation: B forms only 3 bonds using 3 valence electrons, so only 6 electrons (an incomplete octet) surround it in BF$_3$.
questions.trick: 3 bonds using B's 3 valence electrons → only 6 electrons around it.

questions.q: In PCl$_5$, the number of electrons around the central P atom (an example of expanded octet) is
questions.explanation: P forms 5 bonds using empty 3d orbitals, so 10 electrons surround it — an expanded octet.
questions.trick: 5 bonds around P using d orbitals → 10 electrons, expanded octet.

questions.q: Which of the following is an odd-electron molecule that violates the octet rule?
questions.explanation: NO has 11 valence electrons (odd), so one nitrogen electron must remain unpaired, violating the octet rule.
questions.trick: Odd total valence electrons (like NO's 11) always leaves one unpaired.

questions.q: The ammonium ion, NH$_4^+$, is formed when NH$_3$ donates its lone pair to H$^+$. This type of bond is called a
questions.explanation: A coordinate (dative) covalent bond forms when both shared electrons come from one atom (here, the N lone pair).
questions.trick: Both shared electrons from one atom (lone pair donated) → coordinate bond.

questions.q: Among the hydrogen halides, the highest percentage ionic character is shown by
questions.explanation: Ionic character increases with electronegativity difference between the bonded atoms; F is the most electronegative halogen, giving HF the largest $\Delta\chi$ and highest ionic character.
questions.trick: Ionic character rises with electronegativity difference; F is most electronegative → HF highest.

questions.q: The correct order of decreasing carbon–carbon bond length is
questions.explanation: More shared electron pairs pull the bonded atoms closer together, so bond length decreases as bond order increases: single > double > triple.
questions.trick: More bonding pairs pull atoms closer → bond length falls as bond order rises.

questions.q: The total number of sigma and pi bonds in benzene (C$_6$H$_6$) are respectively
questions.explanation: 6 C–C σ bonds (ring) + 6 C–H σ bonds = 12 σ bonds; the 6 delocalised p-electrons form 3 π bonds.
questions.trick: Count $\sigma$ bonds from the skeleton (ring C–C + C–H); delocalised p-electrons give the $\pi$ count.

questions.q: The hybridisation of carbon in CO$_2$ is
questions.explanation: Carbon forms 2 σ bonds with no lone pairs (2 double bonds, O=C=O), giving sp hybridisation and a linear shape.
questions.trick: 2 $\sigma$ bonds, no lone pairs on C → sp, linear O=C=O.

questions.q: The number of sigma and pi bonds in HCN (H–C≡N) are respectively
questions.explanation: H–C is 1 σ bond; C≡N (triple bond) is 1 σ + 2 π bonds. Total: 2 σ and 2 π bonds.
questions.trick: Each bond contributes 1 $\sigma$; a triple bond adds 2 $\pi$ on top.

questions.q: The fundamental postulate of VSEPR theory is that
options: atoms bond only through orbital overlap
bond pairs repel more strongly than lone pairs
electron pairs always pair up with opposite spins
electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves to minimise mutual repulsion
questions.explanation: VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) theory predicts molecular shape by minimising repulsion between electron pairs (bonding and lone) around the central atom.
questions.trick: VSEPR core idea: electron pairs arrange to minimise mutual repulsion.

questions.q: The correct order of increasing bond order among He$_2$, B$_2$, O$_2$ and N$_2$ is
questions.explanation: Bond orders: He$_2$ = 0, B$_2$ = 1, O$_2$ = 2, N$_2$ = 3, giving the increasing order He$_2$ < B$_2$ < O$_2$ < N$_2$.
questions.trick: Recall bond orders directly: He$_2$=0, B$_2$=1, O$_2$=2, N$_2$=3.

questions.q: Among C$_2$, O$_2$, B$_2$ and NO, the diamagnetic species is
questions.explanation: C$_2$ has the configuration $\dots\pi2p_x^2\pi2p_y^2$ with all electrons paired, making it diamagnetic; O$_2$, B$_2$ and NO all have unpaired electrons.
questions.trick: All-paired electron configuration (like C$_2$'s filled $\pi2p$) means diamagnetic.

questions.q: The bond order of the nitrosonium ion, NO$^+$, is
questions.explanation: NO has 15 electrons (bond order 2.5); removing one electron from the antibonding $\pi^*$ orbital to form NO$^+$ gives 14 electrons, isoelectronic with N$_2$, with bond order 3.
questions.trick: Removing an antibonding electron from NO (BO 2.5) raises NO$^+$ to bond order 3.

questions.q: o-Nitrophenol has a lower boiling point than p-nitrophenol mainly because of
options: stronger intermolecular hydrogen bonding in the ortho isomer
intramolecular hydrogen bonding in the ortho isomer preventing association between molecules
higher molecular mass of the ortho isomer
greater ionic character in the ortho isomer
questions.explanation: In o-nitrophenol, the –OH and –NO$_2$ groups form an intramolecular hydrogen bond, so the molecule does not associate with others via intermolecular H-bonding, lowering its boiling point relative to the para isomer.
questions.trick: Intramolecular H-bonding traps the group, blocking intermolecular association → lower b.p.

questions.q: The number of lone pairs on the oxygen atom in a water molecule is
questions.explanation: O has 6 valence electrons; 2 are used in the two O–H bonds, leaving 2 lone pairs.
questions.trick: O uses 2 of its 6 valence electrons in bonds → 2 lone pairs remain.

questions.q: The hybridisation and shape of NH$_4^+$ ion are
questions.explanation: N has 4 bond pairs (3 N–H + 1 coordinate bond to H$^+$) and no lone pair, giving sp$^3$ hybridisation and a regular tetrahedral shape.
questions.trick: 4 bond pairs (incl. coordinate bond), no lone pair → sp$^3$, tetrahedral.

questions.q: cis-1,2-Dichloroethene has a net dipole moment, unlike its trans isomer, because
options: the two C–Cl bond dipoles do not cancel due to the cis arrangement
the two C–Cl bond dipoles cancel completely
questions.explanation: In the cis isomer, both C–Cl bonds point to the same side, so their dipole moment vectors add up instead of cancelling as they do in the symmetric trans isomer.
questions.trick: Same-side (cis) bond dipoles add up instead of cancelling like in trans.

questions.q: A central atom shows a bond angle of 109.5° with no lone pairs on it. Its hybridisation is
questions.explanation: A perfect tetrahedral bond angle of 109.5° with four bond pairs and no lone pairs corresponds to sp$^3$ hybridisation.
questions.trick: 109.5° with zero lone pairs is the sp$^3$ tetrahedral signature angle.
